children.author: colek42
children.text:
I love this. I'm thinking we could make a git trailer of the evidence oid we create -- would make the UX much better.

I maintain witness.dev (CNCF) and cilock.dev (Apache 2.0 open core) that builds provenance around SDLC (or ADLC steps). We are experimenting using this to just let the agents land code after they prove their testing. Right now we are expecting a 2x increase in throughput at the same amount of compute

> 3 -- How many times you have to run that critical path. Most orgs run it 2-3x

This is the one we went after. Our agents have to run tsc, lint and the unit tests before they push (it's in a hook), and CI was then doing all three again from scratch. Now the agent records what it ran as a git trailer on the commit and the PR build skips those steps [1]. Anything headed to main still runs everything, so the trailer only has to be trusted on the intermediate pushes.

Builds went from ~10 minutes to 1.5 over a few weeks, and a good third/half of that was this change. It tends to compound too - getting the build time down led to lower contention, warmer caches, faster throughput. All the usual queuing theory stuff.

[1] https://jonathannen.com/dont-run-it-twice/

We should probably be measuring deployable merges to main. The math just doesn't work for pipeline based CI as you add more agents.

Three things matter.

1 -- How many non-conflicting changes can actually be made at one time (Fan Out)

2 -- How long a critical path takes

3 -- How many times you have to run that critical path. Most orgs run it 2-3x, once before the PR in the agent loop, once in CI, and another in the MQ

This is why most orgs cant get past about 12 PRs an hour.

children.text: When I trimmed my tests, I looked for ones that could be merged. Many unit tests shared the same setup and teardown, so when I merged their middle parts, that setup and teardown only had to run once. Even after merging, the tests still had to stay independent of execution order, so I checked that. In another case, some infrastructure checks were repeated across tests in one folder. children.author: slaser79
children.text: The parity check on test IDs plus the cost cap is a good deterministic checker. For trimming tests, where judgment comes in, I'd have a separate reviewer agent decide it and not the one that proposed the change.

Good question! In terms of the what counts as a win for our agents: speed alone isn't enough. A change only counts if the patched run and the unchanged run executed the same tests (same test IDs, same coverage).

Re-sharding is allowed because it only changes where tests run, not what runs. It has the same sort of parity check as other patches but it also has a cost check to make sure the change doesn't increase runner time by more than 5% by default. We added the cost check after seeing the agents crush wall clock while 10x'ing costs on some test :)

Judging whether or not a test should be trimmed isn't something our agents do yet, because as you alluded to, it's hard. But we're working on it! If you have any ideas or an approach that's worked for you, would love to hear it.

So the agent compares the changed workflow with the existing one and judges whether the speedup is significant. But a change that re-shards or skips tests would always look like a win on speed alone, wouldn't it? How do you check that such changes still catch the bugs the old workflow caught? I had the same worry when I trimmed our tests because CI was too slow.

The parity check — same test IDs, same coverage — answers the "re-sharding vs deleting tests" worry, but it still trusts the test set as the oracle. Is the agent diffing the test bodies as well as the run results? A guard on test-file changes would make the speedup claim much easier to trust.

children.author: devkumardev2001
marcos0811258
children.text:
You're right that file-level sharding is the trap. Setting fullyParallel: true makes Playwright shard individual tests instead of whole files. It balances by test count, not runtime, so your longest-shard tracking still matters.

The totals check gets easier with the blob reporter: run each shard with reporter: 'blob', then npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports. You get one report containing every shard's tests, so a mismatch against --list stands out.

On throttling, workers default to half the logical CPU cores, and the workers option also accepts a percentage. If the count the runner picks is above your CPU limit, timeouts follow. Set workers explicitly in the pod config.

Same test IDs on both runs is the right bar. I’d add one more check before calling a re-shard a win: Playwright shards by file, not by individual test. So equal file counts don’t mean equal workloads. One slow file can dominate a shard, and once it moves, another may become the bottleneck. Track the longest shard’s duration over time, not just the median.

On Bnjoroge’s question, compare the total test count in the merged report with npx playwright test --list on the same commit. That gives you a simple check that the expected tests are represented in the results.

Two lessons from running Playwright in Kubernetes: CPU throttling can cause timeouts that look like flaky tests, so monitor throttling before increasing retries. And keep flaky tests in a separate, non-blocking job rather than letting an optimizer remove them. Otherwise, you improve the metric without fixing the underlying issue.

Disclosure: I work on TestDino, a Playwright reporting tool.

source.text:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

https://starsling.dev

For that optimization, it cut merges to main time in half which is far more than the inference cost us (based on their public usage  https://github.com/chatwoot/chatwoot/actions/metrics/usage?d... ). So short answer is that usually the CI min savings our agent loop finds far outweigh our spend on the optimizations themselves on large repos. On smaller repos less so (I don't have a clear answer on exactly what size). But we also don't charge for optimizations (they're included in runner minutes which are priced the same as competitors) so it's more of an internal question for us we'll figure out as our business matures.

comments.author: yonasb
comments.text: That constant battle you're describing is exactly why having agents part of your hosted runners is valuable. Our agents continuously watch your telemetry, code changes, and runs to find more optimizations. When a PR merges, the agents will catch any regressions and open a fix or revert. Given your past experience, is StarSling solving the drift issue the way you'd want it to be solved? Would love to hear any ideas you have for what the ideal solution would look like.

comments.author: codedrift_
comments.text: I think it's solving some of it, yeah. Most teams never catch it at all, so something watching on merge is huge. About the only thing I'd really pine for is StarSling to also add in regression prevention. If the cause of slowdown has a fix, we should be able to add pre-commit checks that prevent the bad behavior going forward. Otherwise I'm afraid it'll creep back in. Good news though, you can verify that a code check StarSling writes prevents the regression since you've already got all the testing infra built. It's just anything that runs earlier in the process will be cheaper, predictable, and faster.

comments.author: Shexfer
comments.text: The parity check — same test IDs, same coverage — answers the "re-sharding vs deleting tests" worry, but it still trusts the test set as the oracle. The failure I'd want guarded is a change that keeps the same tests but makes them faster by weakening what they assert: a looser timeout, a mocked dependency, a skipped setup. Is the agent diffing the test bodies as well as the run results? A guard on test-file changes would make the speedup claim much easier to trust.

comments.author: devkumardev2001
comments.text: Same test IDs on both runs is the right bar. I’d add one more check before calling a re-shard a win: Playwright shards by file, not by individual test. So equal file counts don’t mean equal workloads. One slow file can dominate a shard, and once it moves, another may become the bottleneck. Track the longest shard’s duration over time, not just the median. On Bnjoroge’s question, compare the total test count in the merged report with npx playwright test --list on the same commit. That gives you a simple check that the expected tests are represented in the results. Two lessons from running Playwright in Kubernetes: CPU throttling can cause timeouts that look like flaky tests, so monitor throttling before increasing retries. And keep flaky tests in a separate, non-blocking job rather than letting an optimizer remove them. Otherwise, you improve the metric without fixing the underlying issue. Disclosure: I work on TestDino, a Playwright reporting tool.

comments.author: marcos0811258
comments.text: You're right that file-level sharding is the trap. Setting fullyParallel: true makes Playwright shard individual tests instead of whole files. It balances by test count, not runtime, so your longest-shard tracking still matters. The totals check gets easier with the blob reporter: run each shard with reporter: 'blob', then npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports. You get one report containing every shard's tests, so a mismatch against --list stands out. On throttling, workers default to half the logical CPU cores, and the workers option also accepts a percentage. If the count the runner picks is above your CPU limit, timeouts follow. Set workers explicitly in the pod config.
